# The exact five-bit count and the coset obstruction at every dimension

For a uniform five-bit permutation the exact probability of failing to mix
on pairs is

$$
\frac{27\,141\,314\,518\,175\,866\,661\,787\,402\,240}{32!}
=\frac{3\,534\,251\,519\,984\,761\,663}
       {34\,264\,020\,623\,061\,220\,992\,000\,000}
=1.03147600769480393\ldots\times 10^{-7}.
$$

Of these nonmixers, exactly $61{,}931{,}520$ are connected and periodic.
The others preserve a nontrivial coset partition. We count **every**
permutation preserving a nontrivial coset partition by the same recurrence
at arbitrary dimension. Beginning at six bits, additional primitive
permutations can fail to mix. The [asymptotic analysis](GROUP_COUNTS.md)
bounds the size of that exceptional family.

## Which maps are counted?

Translate the outputs so that $p(0)=0$. This normalization leaves all
difference transitions and invariant coset partitions unchanged and gives
$N=2^n$ original permutations for each normalized one.

Call a subspace $W$ **invariant** if $p$ permutes its cosets. In derivative
form, $p(x+w)+p(x)\in W$ for all $x$ and $w\in W$. A normalized $p$ is
**simple** here if its only invariant subspaces in this sense are $0$ and $V$.
Equivalently, the group generated by $p$ and the translations is primitive.
The term agrees with simplicity of the algebra $(V,+,p,0)$: its congruence
relations are exactly equality modulo such spaces.
[Published coset criterion, Caranti–Dalla Volta–Sala](https://arxiv.org/abs/0806.4135)

Write $q_n$ for the number of normalized nonlinear simple permutations and
$g_n=|\mathrm{GL}(n,2)|$, with $g_0=1$. The number of simple linear maps is
$\ell_n=g_n I_n/(2^n-1)$ for $n>1$, where $I_n$ is the number of monic
irreducible binary polynomials of degree $n$. Each polynomial gives one
conjugacy class and its centralizer consists of the nonzero field
multiplications. In dimension one take $\ell_1=1$. Thus the exact number of
permutations with a proper nonzero invariant coset partition is

$$
(2^n)!-2^n(q_n+\ell_n).
$$

At three, four and five bits, the earlier dimension-specific results identify
the mixers exactly as the nonlinear simple permutations, up to output
translation. In particular, at five bits $2^5 q_5$ is the full number of
mixers. [Four-bit proof](../FOUR_BIT_COUNT.md) ·
[Five-bit criterion and its six-bit limit](../LARGER_BITS.md#five-bits)

## A signed count from quotient partitions

Let $C(p)$ be the finite lattice of invariant subspaces. Intersections remain
invariant by the derivative criterion. Sums remain invariant by taking
successive shifts from the summands. For any such lattice write $\mu(C)$
for its Möbius function from bottom to top. In the one-element lattice this
value is one.

Use the easily computed numbers

$$
c_d=(2^d)!-\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}[d\;j]_2 c_j((2^{d-j})!)^{2^j}
$$

from [the quotient inclusion–exclusion argument](GROUP_COUNTS.md#a-fixed-order-expansion).
Here $[d\;j]_2$ counts binary subspaces of codimension $j$. The identity we
will need is

$$
-\frac{c_d}{2^d}=\sum_{p(0)=0}\mu(C(p)),\qquad d\ge1.
$$

To verify it, before imposing $p(0)=0$, recall that $c_d$ is the signed sum of
the numbers of permutations preserving each of a family of proper subspaces
with intersection zero. In this definition the zero subspace is allowed.
For a fixed permutation the negative of its contribution is the sum of
$(-1)^{|F|}$ over subsets $F$ of the proper members of $C(p)$ with meet zero.
This is $\mu(C(p))$. Indeed for each $x<V$, the sum without the meet-zero
restriction, over subsets all of whose members contain $x$, is zero by the
binomial theorem. At $x=V$ that sum is one. These are exactly the defining
equations of the Möbius function after grouping by meet and assigning the
empty meet to $V$. Output translations divide the total by $2^d$. This
calculation is an application of lattice Möbius inversion. [Rota, *On the foundations of combinatorial theory I*](https://webhomes.maths.ed.ac.uk/~v1ranick/papers/rota1.pdf)

## Why the signed count separates simple nonlinear maps

**Splitting when the Möbius value is nonzero.** The same binomial argument
works using only the maximal proper members of $C(p)$, because every proper
member lies below one. Thus a nonzero Möbius value implies that some family
of maximal proper invariant subspaces intersects in zero. Choose an
irredundant such family $W_1,\ldots,W_r$. For $r=1$, $W_1=0$ and $p$ is
simple. Otherwise set $B=\bigcap_{i>1}W_i$. Irredundancy gives $B\ne0$;
its intersection with $W_1$ is zero, and maximality of $W_1$ then gives
$V=B\oplus W_1$. Both coordinate coset partitions are preserved.
Normalization implies that $p$ acts separately on the two coordinates. Its
action on $B$ is the quotient $V/W_1$ and is simple.

For each $i>1$, the map $W_1\to V/W_i$ is surjective since $W_1+W_i=V$.
It intertwines the normalized permutations, so $W_1\cap W_i$ is a maximal
proper invariant subspace of $W_1$ by simplicity of this quotient. These
kernels intersect in zero. Iterating on $W_1$ gives a direct sum of simple
coordinate factors. A permutation without such a decomposition has zero
Möbius weight.

**A nonlinear simple factor admits no diagonal congruences.** Suppose $p$
acts as $(b,y)\mapsto(f(b),h(y))$ on $B\oplus Y$, with $f$ nonlinear
simple. For an invariant space $W$, both its projection onto $B$ and
$W\cap B$ are invariant for $f$. For the projection assertion, lift
$u$ in that projection to some $(u,v)\in W$ and take the $B$ coordinate
of the derivative. Thus each of those two spaces is either zero or all of
$B$. If the projection is all of $B$ and the intersection is zero, fix an
arbitrary $u$, a lift $(u,v)$, and a value of $y$. The derivatives based at
$(b,y)$ and $(b',y)$ both lie in $W$ and have the same $Y$ coordinate.
Their difference lies in $W\cap B=0$. Hence $f(b+u)+f(b)$ is independent
of $b$ for every $u$, which would make $f$ linear since $f(0)=0$.

It follows that $W$ either lies in $Y$ or equals $B\oplus(W\cap Y)$. All
such subspaces with $W\cap Y$ invariant do occur. The entire lattice is the
product of the two-element lattice for $B$ and the invariant lattice for
$Y$. Repeating this for all nonlinear factors makes their coordinate
subspaces intrinsic: they are precisely the minimal nonzero invariant
subspaces on which the restriction is nonlinear. The complementary linear
summand is intrinsic as well, since the split lattice shows that it contains
every invariant subspace with linear restriction. Thus different unordered
decompositions into nonlinear simple factors and one remaining linear
summand yield distinct permutations. General results on congruences of
products in Mal'cev varieties provide context for the elementary argument
above. [Mayr–Ruškuc, Lemma 3.3 and the proof of Theorem 4.2](https://arxiv.org/pdf/1604.05408)

**The signed linear mass.** Let $L$ range over the invertible linear maps
on an $m$-space. Sum the alternating-chain formula for $\mu(C(L))$ over these
maps. For a chain $0=U_0<U_1<\cdots<U_r=V$ with fixed intermediate
dimensions, the sum over all such flags of the sizes of their stabilizers is
$g_m$ by orbit–stabilizer. Its sign is $(-1)^r$. There are
$\binom{m-1}{r-1}$ dimension patterns. Hence the sum over $L$ vanishes for
$m\ge2$, equals $-1$ for $m=1$, and equals $1$ for $m=0$.

## The exact recurrence

Möbius functions multiply on direct products of finite lattices, immediately
from their defining equations. A decomposition with $r$ simple nonlinear
factors and a remaining linear map $L$ has weight $(-1)^r\mu(C(L))$.
Every map with nonzero weight is counted by such decompositions. Allowing
arbitrary $L$ includes any additional maps with zero weight automatically.

Suppose there are $k_d$ nonlinear factors of dimension $d$ and the linear
summand has dimension $m=n-\sum_d d k_d$. The number of decompositions into
these actual coordinate subspaces, without an ordering among the nonlinear
factors of each dimension, is

$$
\frac{g_n}{g_m\prod_d g_d^{k_d} k_d!}.
$$

This follows from transitivity of the general linear group on decompositions.
There are $q_d$ choices of normalized nonlinear simple permutation on each
specified $d$-space. Summing over the multiplicities is exactly the formal
power series identity

$$
1-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{c_n z^n}{2^n g_n}
=(1-z)\exp\left(-\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{q_n}{g_n}z^n\right).
$$

This formal coefficient identity computes all $q_n$ successively. The
exponential for unordered labeled direct summands is the classical
finite-vector-space exponential formula. The factor $1-z$ comes from
the signed linear mass computed above. [Morrison, Theorem 8](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0403289)

For an explicit rational-arithmetic
version, set $a_d=c_d/(2^d g_d)$ and

$$
R_d=d a_d+\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}a_j R_{d-j},\qquad
q_d=\frac{g_d}{d}(R_d-1).
$$

These equations follow by taking the logarithmic derivative. All truth tables
on two bits fixing zero are linear. Thus $q_1=q_2=0$. Up to dimension five
there is room for at most one simple nonlinear factor. Since the signed
linear mass vanishes beyond dimension one, in this range the recurrence
simplifies to

$$
q_n=\frac{c_n}{2^n}+(2^n-1)2^{n-1} q_{n-1},\qquad 3\le n\le5.
$$

The second term counts the choices of a nonlinear hyperplane factor and a
complementary line. Evaluating the recurrence gives the following exact
checks and result.

| Bits | Permutations preserving a nontrivial coset partition | Pairwise mixers |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 3 | 7,680 | 32,256 |
| 4 | 48,887,129,088 | 20,873,902,694,400 |
| 5 | 27,141,314,518,175,866,661,725,470,720 | 263,130,809,792,379,011,991,351,350,372,597,760 |

The three-bit census and the earlier four-bit color-partition count provide
independent checks. The exact five-bit fraction also falls within the
independently obtained parity-based bounds. One can exhaustively check the
small-dimensional inputs to the signed argument without enumerating $32!$
permutations. The test suite constructs the complete invariant lattice for all
5,040 normalized three-bit tables and checks the nonlinear product argument
against all 2,825 binary subspaces of a six-bit example. [Arithmetic and small-count checks](group_counts.py) ·
[Independent finite bounds](GROUP_COUNTS.md#five-bits-with-finite-bounds)

The labeled-coset counting recurrence for a uniform repeated permutation and
